title: New Swift packages add open-model choices for speech and decisions
dek: Two new Swift libraries let app developers swap speech engines and request typed model decisions, but hardware requirements and confidence scores still need careful testing.
whatHappened: On October 29, 2026, developer Mattt announced AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel in a Hugging Face blog post; these are independent packages, not new Apple products.
AnySpeechRecognizer follows Apple's modern Speech API while adding selectable engines, including local Parakeet and Qwen3-ASR, and speaker diarization.
AnyDecisionModel returns probabilities and typed choices or scores instead of requiring applications to parse generated answer text. Its repository documents local and hosted backends.
whyItMatters: Comparison checked October 31: Apple's WWDC25 documentation describes on-device SpeechTranscriber with system-managed model assets and updates. AnySpeechRecognizer instead offers engine choice behind a similar interface; its README requires Swift 6.2 and macOS 26 or iOS 26, with Apple silicon for Parakeet and Sortformer.

The creator's October 29 comparison distinguishes live Parakeet output with word timing from Qwen3-ASR's segment-final output without word timing or confidence. That is a product-design tradeoff, not a universal accuracy ranking; the reported speech tests ran on a Mac, not an iPhone.

For routing and scoring applications, typed decisions remove a text-parsing step. The decision-library README warns that confidence reflects the concentration of probabilities, not the chance an answer is correct, and that confidence values should not be compared across backends.

Open-model flexibility adds integration work: the decision README says hosted wire compatibility was checked against fixtures rather than live services, and calibration transfer to new tasks is untested. Teams still need domain-specific evaluations before automating consequential actions.
take: The speech package is useful when engine choice or speaker attribution is worth more than the simplicity of a system-managed model; Apple's native path remains a sensible baseline rather than an obsolete option.
Typed decisions can make application code cleaner, but a well-formed answer is not evidence of a well-calibrated or instruction-resistant decision.
Builders should compare complete workflows on their target devices, including model downloads, latency and error rates, before treating a shared Swift interface as interchangeable behavior.
openQuestions: How do the speech engines perform on supported iPhones and on an application's real languages, microphones and overlapping speakers?
Will calibration and hosted integrations remain reliable outside the repository's tested tasks and fixtures?

sources.title: Bring advanced speech-to-text to your app with SpeechAnalyzer, WWDC25; checked October 31, 2026
